verses.translation_literal: Praise [you all] Yah! Praise [you], my soul, [obj] YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hallelujah! Praise the LORD, all of you. And you, my soul, you above all: rise up and praise the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a double summons. The first command is plural and goes out to the congregation: halelu-yah, the word that has become 'hallelujah' in every language and means, plainly, 'praise Yah'. Then the singer turns inward and gives a second command, in the feminine singular, to his own nefesh: haleli nafshi. Nefesh is the whole living self, the throat that breathes and the appetite that hungers, not a ghost inside a body. So the speaker talks to himself, the way a person bracing for a long day tells himself to get up. Ibn Ezra hears two voices here, the poet to Israel, and then to his own soul.

The KJV 'Praise ye the Lord' is accurate, but it hides the change of number between the two imperatives, and the KJV prints 'the Lord' where the Hebrew has the four-letter name YHWH in the second half. The psalm that follows is going to say that you should not trust princes. This opening already shows what to do instead: spend your own breath on praise.

philological_notes.note: A plural imperative plus Yah, the short form of the divine name. The Masoretes write it as one hyphenated unit but the text still counts it as two words. Psalms 146 to 150 each open and close with it.
'My soul', but nefesh is the living self, throat and breath included. Addressing it as a second person is the psalmist's way of rousing himself.

verses.translation_literal: I will praise YHWH in my lives; I will sing to my God in my still-being.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will praise the LORD as long as I have life. I will sing to my God for as long as there is any of me left to sing.
verses.directors_commentary:
The soul has been told what to do, and now the singer answers with a vow. Two time phrases carry it. Be-chayyai is literally 'in my lives': chayyim, 'life', is a plural form in Hebrew, and here it takes a first-person ending. Be-'odi is 'in my still-ness', 'in my yet-being', from 'od, 'still, yet'. Malbim hears two gifts in the pair: life itself, and the extra, the 'yet' that God goes on granting after it. Whether or not one takes the distinction that far, the effect is a vow that runs out only when the singer does. It also prepares the next verse, where the prince's breath will go out and his plans with it.

The KJV 'while I live ... while I have any being' gets the sense but turns two nouns into verbs and softens the 'still' in 'od. The two verbs differ as well. Halal is praise by voice, and zimmer is song with an instrument, as Metzudat David glosses the two (by mouth; with musical instruments). The divine titles vary too: YHWH first, then 'my God', which Malbim reads as the more personal one.

philological_notes.note: 'In my lives': the plural of chayyim with a suffix. The plural is the ordinary Hebrew way to say 'life', and means the whole span.
'While I am still': 'od is 'yet, still, again'. Malbim takes it as the surplus God grants beyond bare life.
Cohortative of zimmer, 'make music, sing praise'. Metzudat David ties it to instruments, in contrast to halal, which he ties to the mouth.

verses.translation_literal: Do not trust in nobles, in a son of man to whom there is no deliverance.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not put your trust in princes. Do not lean on a mortal man: he has no power to save you.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here is the turn. The psalm has just given its own breath to God, and now it says what not to do with yours. Nedivim are the 'willing, generous, noble ones': the great men of a city, patrons who could open a door or a granary. In a world with no state welfare and no courts for the poor, a nadiv was the person you went to when the harvest failed or a creditor came. The warning is not that such men are cruel. The warning is that they are men.

The Hebrew is blunt: ben-adam, 'son of man', is simply a human being, a child of the ground ('adamah, which returns in the next verse). Tesh'uah is 'deliverance', the same word as 'salvation'; the KJV 'no help' flattens it, and BBE's 'no salvation' keeps the weight. The grammar is also compressed: 'in a son of man' follows 'in nobles' with no 'nor', which the KJV supplies. Ibn Ezra says the man 'cannot even save himself'; Malbim notes that even a willing patron's power is not his own.

philological_notes.note: From the root of willingness: 'those who volunteer', hence noble, generous, a patron class. Meiri glosses it as officers and the honored.
Deliverance, rescue, salvation. It is the same root as the name Joshua/Jesus. The psalm says no human can supply it, and goes on to say who can.

verses.translation_literal: His breath goes out; he returns to his ground; on that day his plans perish.
verses.translation_dramatic: His breath slips out of him, and he goes back to the ground he came from. And on that very day every plan he ever made is gone.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reason the verse before gave. The prince's breath, his ruach, 'goes out', and the man 'returns to his ground'. The echo is deliberate: ben-'adam, son of man, goes back to 'adamah, soil, the old Genesis wordplay of the human who is made from earth and goes back to it. Malbim cites 'the dust returns to the earth and the spirit returns' (Ecclesiastes 12:7) as the model, and Radak adds the sharp point: a man does not even control when his own breath leaves him.

Then comes a rare word: 'eshtonotav, 'his plans'. Rashi simply glosses it 'his thoughts'; Ibn Ezra links it to the verb in Jonah 1:6, 'perhaps God will give thought to us', the same root used there. The KJV 'his thoughts perish' is right in sense, but 'plans, schemes' is closer to what a powerful man does with his thinking. The timing is stressed: 'on that day', not eventually. A promise made by a patron dies with him, and whatever he meant to do for you dies in the same hour. In the KJV 'in that very day' adds an intensifier the Hebrew only implies by the demonstrative.

philological_notes.note: 'His thoughts, his plans'. A rare word tied to the root 'sht, 'to think, to give thought'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as thoughts, with Metzudat Zion citing Jonah 1:6.
Breath, wind, spirit: all one word. English has to choose, and the KJV chose 'breath', which fits the verb 'goes out'.
'To his ground'. The 'adam/'adamah pun of the creation story, here with 'ben-'adam' just before.

verses.translation_literal: Happy [is he] whom the God of Jacob [is] in his help, his hope [is] upon YHWH his God.
verses.translation_dramatic: But happy, how happy, is the one whose help is the God of Jacob, the one whose hope rests on the LORD, his God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns on this word. Verses 3–4 ended in a grave: the prince's breath leaves him, his plans die with him. Now comes אַשְׁרֵי, 'ashrei, and it should land like a door opening. Play it as a cry, not as a mild remark. The word is a plural construct, 'the blessednesses of', so the plain sense is 'oh, the happinesses of the man who…'. The KJV's tidy 'Happy is he' flattens that overflow. Metzudat David reads 'ashrei as serving two clauses at once: happy is the one whose help is the God of Jacob, and happy is the one whose hope is on YHWH.

Why Jacob, of all patriarchs? He is the man who ran from his brother with nothing, a stone for a pillow, and was promised 'I am with you and will keep you' (Gen 28:15, the verse Rashi cites). Radak likewise makes him the model of trust in flight. The audience, in exile or just back from it, hears their own story. The KJV supplies 'hath… for his help', turning a verbless line into a possession; the Hebrew has no verb, only 'the God of Jacob [is] in his help', God standing inside the helping. And על is 'upon': his hope is laid on YHWH as weight on a beam, where the KJV's 'in' is softer.

philological_notes.note: Plural construct of 'esher, 'happiness', so literally 'the happinesses of'. It opens Psalm 1 and the whole Psalter's blessing vocabulary. Metzudat David reads it as governing both clauses of the verse: happy is the one whose help is the God of Jacob, and happy is the one whose hope is on YHWH.

'His hope', a noun from the root of 'looking expectantly'. It is not the common שבר 'to break', though the consonants are the same; the hearer may catch the echo of brokenness and its opposite. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'his hope'.

verses.translation_literal: Maker of heaven and earth, [obj] the sea and [obj] all that is in them; the keeper of faithfulness for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the maker of heaven and earth, of the sea and of everything that moves in them. And He keeps faith, and He will keep it for ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
The next lines give the reasons for the blessing, and they are a list of what God does. The first is the largest: he made 'heaven and earth', and then, as if the singer cannot stop, 'the sea and everything in them'. Radak notes that 'earth' means dry land, which is why the sea needs naming separately. Rashi, on this chapter, uses the list to make the contrast the psalm is drawing: a king who worships idols may be able to guard you on land but cannot guard you at sea, while the Maker of the sea can guard you in both. In the surrounding world the sea was a god or a chaos-monster; here it is simply something that was made.

The second claim is about reliability. 'Emet is not only 'truth' but 'faithfulness', 'what holds', from the root that gives 'amen'. The KJV 'keepeth truth' sounds like doctrine, while the Hebrew describes a keeper of promises. Rashi reads it as keeping a promise across many generations, and Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read it as keeping what he promised. After verse 4, where a man's promises die with him, the contrast is complete.

philological_notes.note: Faithfulness, reliability, what is firm; the same root as 'amen'. 'Truth' in the KJV loses the sense of keeping one's word.
A participle with the article, 'the one keeping'. The same root is used in verse 9, 'YHWH watches over the sojourners'.

verses.translation_literal: Doer of justice for the oppressed, giver of bread to the hungry; YHWH looser of the bound.
verses.translation_dramatic: He does justice for those who are crushed. He gives bread to the hungry. The LORD sets the prisoners free.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the cosmos the psalm drops to the street, and the three things it names are the three things a poor person in a hard city could not get from a patron: a fair hearing, a meal, and release. 'Ashuqim are those who are 'oppressed' or defrauded: the root is about extortion, taking by force what belongs to another, as in a landlord who takes the field or a creditor who takes the son. Metzudat Zion says it means 'the robbed'. Mishpat is more than a verdict: it is the right outcome, the thing put right.

The food is lechem, 'bread', which in the ancient world is simply food, the daily grain ration; the KJV 'food' is acceptable. The prisoners are 'asurim, 'the bound', people in debt-bondage or in a pit or a prison, and the verb mattir means to untie, as Metzudat David says, 'to open the knots'. Note that the divine name comes only at the start of the third line: the first two are participles with no subject, so the sentence builds toward it. Malbim makes the sharp observation that a human king who frees a prisoner thinks he has done enough, but YHWH also sees to the justice and the bread afterward.

philological_notes.note: 'The oppressed, the defrauded': those from whom something has been taken by force or fraud. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'the robbed'.
A hiphil participle, 'one who loosens, unties'. Metzudat David says it means opening the knots that bind the prisoners and sending them out free.
'The bound': prisoners or debtors. Meiri reads both literal prison and the 'prison of troubles'.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH opening the blind; YHWH raising the bowed; YHWH loving the righteous.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD opens the eyes of the blind. The LORD lifts up those who are bent double. The LORD loves the righteous.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three short clauses, and each begins with the name, YHWH, YHWH, YHWH, like three strokes of a bell. Nothing here is subordinate: it is a litany, and the actor should let each name land before the verb. The verbs are participles, so there is no 'once' or 'will': this is what he is doing, as a habit and a character.

The KJV 'openeth the eyes of the blind' supplies 'the eyes', as the Hebrew has only 'opening blind people' (poqeach 'ivrim). Poqeach is the verb for opening eyes in Isaiah 42:7, as Metzudat Zion notes. Radak reads the blindness as either an eye disease or the darkness of trouble, and Malbim as both bodily and mental. 'Kefufim' are the bowed, those bent over by weight or poverty or shame, and Metzudat David says God raises them to stand upright. The last clause moves from what he does to who he loves, and Ibn Ezra reads that love as protection: the righteous will not be oppressed, hungry, bound, blind or bowed.

philological_notes.note: 'Opening' (of eyes or ears). The usual verb for opening the eyes, as in Isaiah 42:7, which Metzudat Zion cites.
'The bent down, the bowed': bent by poverty, grief or heavy work. Radak understands them as the poor; Malbim as bowed by humility or by poverty.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH [is] keeping the sojourners; fatherless and widow he sustains, and the way of [the] wicked he makes crooked.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD stands guard over the stranger far from home. The orphan and the widow he lifts back onto their feet. And the road of the wicked? That he bends, and bends again, until it will not carry them where they meant to go.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four kinds of people stand in front of you, and three of them have no one: the sojourner (גֵּר, ger), the fatherless child, the widow. In the ancient Near East a family, a clan and a plot of land were a person's only insurance. Without them a person had no voice at the gate and no portion at harvest. Deuteronomy names exactly these three again and again as the ones the community must feed and protect. Ibn Ezra and Radak say the same: they have no helper, so God is their helper. The KJV's 'strangers' loses the legal sense: a ger is a resident alien without land or kin, not a passer-by.

The verse ends on a sharp contrast the KJV overplays. 'He turneth upside down' is too violent. The Hebrew יְעַוֵּת says he makes the way crooked, bent out of true: the wicked still walk, but the road no longer goes where they planned. Ibn Ezra hears schemes and circumstances that frustrate them; Metzudat David hears something sharper, that God puts it in their heart to choose the path that ruins them. Note the grammar: the object marker אֶת appears only with the sojourners; orphan and widow are fronted for emphasis before their verb. And note the wordplay: the same God who straightens the bent (v. 8) bends the road of the wicked.

philological_notes.note: A polel form, 'he restores, lifts, sustains'; STEPBible has 'helps up'. Rashi glosses it as strength, Radak as 'lifted up', and Metzudat Zion as raising and strengthening, comparing 'and we have risen and been lifted up' (Ps 20:9). The picture is of setting a fallen person back on their feet.

Piel of עָוַת, 'to bend, make crooked, twist'. Metzudat Zion derives it from 'distortion and crookedness'. It is gentler than the KJV's 'turneth upside down': the road is bent, not overturned. Meiri takes it as 'twisted and curved'. The verse sets this against v. 8, where God straightens the bent.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH will reign for ever, your God, O Zion, to a generation and a generation. Praise Yah!
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD will reign for ever. Your God, O Zion, will reign from one generation to the next. Hallelujah!
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a royal verdict. Against the princes of verse 3, who die and whose plans die with them, stands the king who does not. The verb is imperfect, 'he will reign' or 'reigns', and it is paired with two time phrases: 'for ever' (le'olam) and 'to a generation and a generation' (ledor vador). Malbim reads a distinction in them, with 'for ever' as the unbroken age and the pair of generations as time divided into successive turns, each one met by God anew. The pair also answers verse 4: one man's day ends, and this king's generations do not.

Then the address shifts: 'your God, O Zion', with a feminine singular suffix, because Zion is a woman, a city spoken to as a person. The KJV 'even thy God' adds 'even'; the Hebrew simply lays the name next to the city. Zion is also where the psalm's powerless find a King who will do justice, and the reader hears the whole weight of the lists above as his policy. The closing 'Praise Yah!' matches the opening frame, so the psalm is a circle: praise, warning, reasons, reign, praise. Radak hears the verse as the hope of the day when all the world will acknowledge his kingship.

philological_notes.note: 'Your God, O Zion': the suffix is feminine singular, addressing the city as a woman. Malbim reads this as the special bond between God and Zion, apart from his rule over all creation.
'To a generation and a generation': a doubled phrase meaning 'through all generations'. Malbim distinguishes it from le'olam as time that comes in successive turns.
